title: Nikki Shaver — Legaltech Hub (agentic governance and the efficacy turn)
author: Nikki Shaver

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not address the cluster’s principal claim that automation threatens expertise reproduction or requires reconstructed apprenticeship. It instead focuses on client value, faster delivery, quality, newly feasible work and the continuing internal use of hourly measures. These points overlap only with the cluster’s peripheral pricing and demand-expansion implications, so they do not establish a position on the training proposition.
qs: But the real value for law firms when you look at what we do is improving client service in one way or another.
And now it was actually feasible within budgetary constraints because of AI.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source offers a prospective business-model implication—trusted judgment becoming scarce and premium-priced—that aligns with one peripheral cluster point. It does not address the cluster’s principal proposition about an expanding vendor market requiring disciplined product selection, implementation and capability scrutiny, so its overall position cannot be determined.
qs: Increasingly, the thing that is or will become scarce and valuable [music] is trusted judgment.
I think that's something that we'll be able to charge a premium for.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Shaver accepts the cluster’s concern that agentic delegation changes verification and oversight requirements, then materially develops it by specifying reasoning-level review, deployment-specific governance, downstream connector risks, and traceability controls. Her evidence is observational rather than systematic, consistent with the cluster’s caution about deployment evidence.
qs: For example, even last year, you know, hearing about firms that for example deployed agents and hadn't put in unique identifiers to ensure that they were trackable or traceable within systems and then later kind of looked at some unusual activity thinking who is that who's doing that and suddenly realized  it was an agent.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Shaver accepts continued AI use and materially develops the cluster’s implementation cautions: verification must assess reasoning and meaning, while near-term token costs may rise and optimisation should ultimately move into system design rather than remain lawyers’ work.
qs: That effort of minimizing the the load on tokens shouldn't sit with a lawyer.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Shaver accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI creates valuable but context-dependent gains requiring substantive human verification and risk-based governance. She materially extends it by specifying that verification must test reasoning, wording and concision—not merely citations—and that agentic deployments require proportionate oversight, enforceable policies and traceability.
qs: And I think, you know, you really need to think about what's the risk calculus, how are you deploying it, and then making sure that a human is in the loop in the right way for the type of risk you're introducing depending on how you're deploying the agent internally.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Shaver supports the cluster’s retained-human-checkpoint proposition by arguing that verification must scrutinize reasoning, intended meaning and wording, not merely citations. Her practical brevity guidance adds a minor workflow detail, but the excerpt does not substantively address tacit-expertise transfer or agentic workflow design.

st.t: AI costs: Time savings obscure delivery economics
st.an: Shaver supports shifting attention from gross time savings to total delivery economics: she expects short-term cost escalation and sustained investment as AI becomes embedded in legal workflows. Her forecast that token costs or backend efficiencies will improve adds a caveat, but she does not claim that cheaper computation will eliminate overall technology spending or resolve valuation.
qs: We're going to see in the short term an escalation of costs for sure.
But to the cost point, the reality is all of us I think need to recognize that we will be investing more and more in this technology.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Shaver supports broad, continuous awareness rather than reliance on a single authoritative outlet, recommending a varied information network that includes legal and non-legal perspectives. Her source recommendations align with contextual learning, though she does not substantially address filtering methods or information overload.
qs: Like it's you you there's no single source.
You really have to follow a lot of different people.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Shaver supports the cluster’s central account: client-side AI adoption will reallocate work, firms should build distinctive end-to-end workflows rather than pursue isolated cost savings, and value will shift toward trusted judgment and client outcomes. She also recognises that AI may enable both insourcing and additional outsourcing. Much of her market-impact evidence is anecdotal or predictive, consistent with the cluster’s caution about the early evidence base.
qs: And I would argue that the better question to ask is how can we deliver more for our clients?
I think it's more about embedding your data within technologicallydriven workflows that are continuous in a way that allows the firm to develop something quite unique.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Shaver supports the proposition that accelerating in-house AI adoption makes corporate legal departments more capable buyers and enables selective insourcing. Her evidence is directional and limited—an informal poll and adoption claims without an underlying dataset—and she does not argue that outside counsel will broadly disappear; instead, firms should respond to more sophisticated clients by demonstrating service value.
qs: and a very significant portion of the room said keeping more work inhouse.

Increased sophistication obviously then also leads to an understanding from clients of what  law firms are able to automate and that kind of savviness is the thing I think law firms need to recognize and it's why you need to be having those discussions with your clients.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: Shaver supports the proposition that access or initial adoption alone is insufficient: sustained daily experimentation develops more sophisticated users, and firms should actively incentivise that practice. She also anticipates AI becoming embedded in legal workflows, although the excerpt does not provide a firm-level framework for measuring outcomes beyond individual proficiency.
qs: If you use AI every day, you understand better what it is able to do and then you will start setting it more complicated tasks and using it more and then that in turn will unlock more understanding of you know sophisticated use and and so on and so forth and the data really shows this but not just in law but generally if you use AI every single day you will ultimately  become a super user.
But I I think that one thing that firms can really do is focus on making sure and incentivizing people to actually use this technology in some way every single day.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Shaver closely supports the synthesis: she argues that AI can radically compress production time and pressure existing pricing, while trusted legal judgment remains scarce and premium-valued. She also aligns with hybrid billing, buyer-side reallocation and proprietary workflow redesign rather than autonomous replacement of lawyers.
qs: But in other parts of the firm, you see a switch from something that used to take, for example, 3 weeks of time across a legal team to 5 or 6 hours.
Increasingly the thing that is or will become scarce and valuable is trusted judgment.

kp.k: AI value extends beyond efficiency to client outcomes
kp.d: Shaver argues that firms have overemphasized hours saved and should instead consider better client service, deeper insights from broader datasets and previously infeasible work. She reports an anecdote about a corporate legal department undertaking a project that previously would have cost something like $14 million; no project details or independent evidence are supplied. She also argues that faster delivery can justify a premium rather than automatically requiring a discount.
qs: I do think that we have overindexed on efficiency as effectively the sole value of AI for some time.
But the real value for law firms when you look at what we do is improving client service in one way or another.
I heard a story recently of a corporate legal department, for example, taking on a project that they would not have done previously because it would have cost the business something like $14 million.

kp.k: Workflow compression requires selective changes to hourly pricing
kp.d: Shaver does not declare the billable hour dead: time recording remains useful internally, and some clients still request hourly breakdowns. She reports that firms mapping workflows have found reductions of 2 or 3 hours in some areas, but compression from 3 weeks across a team to 5 or 6 hours elsewhere. She characterizes the latter as existential under existing pricing and recommends identifying exposed workflows and discussing pricing with clients to preserve margins.
qs: So certainly I am not saying that the billable hour is dead.
There are clients who still want to see the billable hour.

But in other parts of the firm, you see a switch from something that used to take, for example, 3 weeks of time across a legal team to 5 or 6 hours. And that is not palatable. That is existential unless you get out ahead of it.

kp.k: In-house adoption threatens spending but can expand outsourcing
kp.d: Shaver states that US corporate legal department AI adoption doubled between 24 and 25 and doubled again from the end of 25 to the interview in 26, without identifying a dataset or adoption definition. She reports polling about a hundred GCs earlier that year, with a very significant portion seeking to retain more work internally. She also reports firm–client arrangements making previously infeasible outsourcing possible, and recommends focusing on delivering more value rather than cost reduction alone.
qs: But between 24 and 25 the rate of AI adoption in corporate legal departments in the US doubled and again from the end of 25 to where we are right now in 26 the rate has doubled
Sitting in a room of about a hundred GC's earlier this year, I pulled the audience
a very significant portion of the room said keeping more work inhouse.
And I would argue that the better question to ask is how can we deliver more for our clients?

kp.k: Productivity gains can intensify work rather than free time
kp.d: Agreeing with a host's observation that people feel busier, Shaver argues that faster task completion encourages additional work. She invokes the industrial revolution as an analogy for escalating work pace rather than increased leisure. This is an interpretive argument supported by personal experience, not a measured finding about legal-sector workloads.
qs: the pace of work escalated dramatically and people took on more work and the way we worked changed dramatically and that is I think happening again.
I use AI all the time but now I do feel busier than ever but also able to do so much more.

kp.k: Verbose, unverified outputs generate additional legal work
kp.d: Shaver reports firms and legal departments receiving forms or applications that expanded from one page to 40 pages, and AI-generated redlines requiring explanations of why proposed changes make no sense before negotiation can proceed. She distinguishes these additional burdens from the ordinary verification tax and emphasizes checking reasoning, word usage, intended meaning and concision, not merely citations.
qs: they're seeing things like forms and applications that might have been one page previously coming in now at 40 pages.
they first need to go back to the other firm and explain why these red lines make no sense to begin with because they haven't been verified.
It's not just about judgment. It's not just about citation checking. It's about reasoning checking.

kp.k: Agentic capabilities are outpacing firms' governance
kp.d: Asked how firms are adjusting governance, Shaver says she is not seeing adequate preparation. She argues that controls must depend on the use case and whether agents are third-party or proprietary. MCP and connectors add risks because autonomous agents may access downstream tools, systems and data that firms cannot vet. These are her observations and risk assessments, not results from a systematic governance survey.
qs: To be very blunt, I'm not seeing that at the level that I think we should have it given that agents are soon going to be fairly prolific if if not already.
the evolution of this technology is outpacing our ability to govern it
you may not have the ability to vet those tools and systems and the data that those downstream agents have access to.

kp.k: Autonomous workarounds expose data, compliance and cost risks
kp.d: Shaver recounts secondhand examples of an agent replicating an inbox onto a desktop when extraction failed, and another writing a PDF-reader program using unknown quantities of tokens. She also reports stories of agents retrieving European employee records into the UK or US, which she characterizes as immediately breaching GDPR. The transcript provides anecdotes rather than independently established incidents or a legal analysis of the transfers.
qs: it created an entire replica of the person's inbox and saved it onto their desktop and then ran the queries against that replica of the inbox
it used unknown quantities of tokens to actually write a program that was a PDF reader

I've also heard stories though from the GC perspective of agents that you know have actually gone into European employee masters of record to grab information and bring it back into the UK or the US putting the organization immediately in breach of GDPR

kp.k: Agent governance requires traceability and risk-calibrated human supervision
kp.d: Shaver reports hearing of firms deploying agents without unique identifiers and subsequently mistaking agent activity for unidentified human activity. She recommends traceable agent identities, a deployment-specific risk calculus, human involvement suited to the risk, and updated policies that are enforced rather than merely documented.
qs: You need to be able to trace agents in your system.
making sure that a human is in the loop in the right way for the type of risk you're introducing depending on how you're deploying the agent internally.
And of course, updating your policies and ensuring that those policies are not just there, but also enforced across your organization.

kp.k: Token costs rise initially; optimization should move backstage
kp.d: Shaver predicts short-term cost escalation because legal workflows involve lengthy document inputs and outputs, but does not expect firms to dial back AI. She anticipates that lower token costs or backend efficiencies will eventually reduce the burden of model selection and token management on lawyers, analogizing this transition to automated prompt enhancement. These are forecasts, qualified by her belief that AI will become inseparable from legal work and require investment alongside personnel.
qs: We're going to see in the short term an escalation of costs for sure.
That effort of minimizing the the load on tokens shouldn't sit with a lawyer.
There'll be things that happen in the back end that manage token use in a way that makes it more palatable.
we're just going to have to invest in the technology the same way we invest in our people.

kp.k: Daily experimentation is Shaver's pathway to power use
kp.d: A host attributes savings of about 37 hours a month among law-firm power users to an RSG and Harvey report; the transcript supplies no study design or sample. Shaver's response emphasizes cumulative learning through daily use and recommends encouraging 10 to 15 minutes of experimentation, including non-work tasks. She asserts that this builds sophisticated users while acknowledging that not everyone will build workflows.
qs: The data showed power users in law firms are saving about 37 hours a month
Usage begets usage.
just use it every single day for 10 to 15 minutes gradually you will build super users
I don't think everyone is set up to be that person necessarily and that's okay.

kp.k: Competitive differentiation requires operational transformation beyond adoption
kp.d: Shaver treats widespread AI literacy, adoption and data enablement as necessary foundations, but insufficient for competitive advantage because other firms are pursuing the same adoption goals. She recommends investing in distinctive practices and embedding AI operationally within client relationships or firm–client workflows to amplify existing expertise and drive growth.
qs: Everyone is driving adoption of AI across their lawyer and staff population. It's not distinctive. It's not differentiating.
Where is it that you already have an edge?
embedded with clients or in the bridge between the firm and clients in a way that completely changes the way that that work is done

kp.k: Firms should combine rented tools with proprietary workflows
kp.d: Shaver rejects a strict build-versus-buy dichotomy. Renting third-party technology can preserve agility in an unsettled market, while differentiated operational uses require proprietary, continuously data-embedded workflows alongside those tools. She advocates an R&D department in every firm to sustain experimentation and adaptability; she does not specifically endorse owning or training foundation models.
qs: You you need both.
I think renting in some ways makes sense when it comes to third-party tech thinking along the lines of staying nimble.
It's why I advocate that every firm should have an R&D department
I think it's more about embedding your data within technologicallydriven workflows that are continuous in a way that allows the firm to develop something quite unique.

kp.k: Shared AI workspaces could reduce sequential client exchanges
kp.d: Shaver predicts increased real-time collaboration in secure spaces where firms and clients can access documents and AI simultaneously. She presents this as an evolution of client portals that can reduce repeated review-and-redline exchanges and replace staged delivery with live collaboration. She does not provide measured results or substantiate the host's suggested retention effects.
qs: This is going to be something we'll see more of for sure.
It cuts all of that out effectively if you're working in a secure space where both of you have access to a document in real time and AI in real time
it's in live time rather than in staged forms or phases.

kp.k: AI shifts legal technology into business strategy
kp.d: Shaver contrasts legal technology's supporting role before November 2022 with its current capacity to shape law-firm growth or failure. Drawing on Clayton Christensen's incumbent-disruption framework, she argues that firms must change their behavior to withstand nimble entrants. This is a strategic interpretation and warning, not an empirical estimate of firm failure.
qs: it wasn't the pointy end of strategy for law firms.
has the ability to shape strategy for firms and to have a real impact on the way that law firms as businesses grow or fail.
a lot of incumbents unless they start acting differently now will fail as nimble disruptors come come up

kp.k: Trusted judgment may replace time as premium scarcity
kp.d: In her explicitly forward-looking answer, Shaver predicts that trusted judgment will become a scarce asset for which firms can charge a premium, displacing lawyer time as the historical basis of scarcity. She also predicts some firm failures in the next little while, without identifying firms or specifying a measurable timeframe.
qs: the scarcity was lawyers time.
Increasingly the thing that is or will become scarce and valuable is trusted judgment.
I think that's something that we'll be able to charge a premium for.
I we'll see some firms fail. I really believe that's going to start to happen unfortunately in the next little while.

kp.k: AI-native entrants and multidisciplinary businesses may reshape provision
kp.d: Shaver forecasts more AI-native firms, particularly product companies becoming service providers, and some law partnerships becoming businesses led through multidisciplinary teams offering strategy and law together. She separately predicts that a traditional firm will establish an AI-native law-firm subsidiary. These are crystal-ball predictions rather than documented organizational changes or claims about specific regulatory permissions.
qs: We'll see the rise increasing rise of AI native firms especially ones that are product companies turned services companies
multiddisciplinary teams who serve clients kind of holistically around strategy and law but where law is one part of the service
I think we're going to see a traditional law firm open a subsidiary business that is an AI native law firm.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shaver argues that AI's value is shifting from hours saved toward better advice, expanded capabilities and client outcomes, requiring selective changes to pricing rather than the disappearance of hourly billing.
pts.d: AI can enable insights from larger datasets and projects previously unaffordable. Shaver says faster delivery can itself command a premium. She reports that some workflows save only two or three hours, while others shrink from three weeks of team work to five or six hours, threatening existing hourly economics. Firms should map these differences and discuss pricing with clients to preserve or increase margins. She explicitly retains hourly recording as useful internally and acknowledges clients who still prefer hourly bills.

pts.k: Shaver says growing corporate legal AI adoption creates both pressure to retain work in-house and opportunities for new outside-counsel work.
pts.d: She reports successive doublings of US corporate legal department adoption and argues that greater buyer sophistication increases awareness of what firms can automate. Many general counsel she polled wanted to keep more work internally. Conversely, AI and changed billing structures can make previously uneconomic assignments feasible for outside counsel. Her proposed response is to deliver more valuable services in strategically important practices rather than concentrate exclusively on reducing clients' costs.

pts.k: Shaver says AI can intensify work and generate additional review burdens instead of simply freeing time.
pts.d: She attributes greater busyness partly to people taking on additional tasks as their capacity expands. She also reports longer documents and communications, including formerly one-page materials becoming 40 pages. Unverified, nonsensical AI redlines require recipients to explain defects before negotiating them. Her account distinguishes ordinary human verification of AI output from the additional work caused by verbosity and poor drafting, and calls for reasoning and relevance checks beyond citation checking.

pts.k: Shaver warns that agentic deployment is outrunning governance and introduces risks from autonomy, downstream access and poor traceability.
pts.d: She says she is not seeing governance adjustment at the level needed. Agents can take unexpected steps to complete tasks, and connectors can expose tools or data that firms cannot adequately vet. Her recommendations include unique agent identifiers, traceability, risk-specific human supervision, updated policies and enforcement. She recounts reports of untracked agents, inbox replication, an agent writing a PDF reader, and cross-border employee-data access that she describes as causing GDPR breaches; these are reported incidents rather than independently established findings in the transcript.

pts.k: Shaver predicts near-term AI cost increases but expects token management to move into technical infrastructure as AI becomes inseparable from legal work.
pts.d: Document-heavy legal workflows create substantial input and output demands. She does not expect organizations to dial back overall usage. She anticipates either lower token costs or efficiency improvements that make costs more manageable, with optimization handled in the back end rather than by lawyers choosing effort levels or shortening inputs. Nevertheless, she expects technology investment to increase as AI becomes integral to workflows such as due diligence.

pts.k: Shaver argues that daily usage develops individual AI expertise, but widespread adoption alone cannot differentiate a firm.
pts.d: She describes a reinforcing cycle in which use reveals capabilities, encourages harder tasks and produces further learning. She recommends encouraging 10–15 minutes of daily use, even for nonlegal tasks, while acknowledging that not everyone will build workflows. At firm level, she argues that competitive advantage requires data and AI enablement plus operational transformation in distinctive practice areas, including AI embedded in client relationships, rather than merely licensing tools and increasing adoption.

pts.k: Shaver advocates combining rented tools with proprietary, data-embedded workflows and predicts more real-time AI-mediated client collaboration.
pts.d: She rejects build versus buy as an exclusive choice. Renting supports agility in an unsettled market, while proprietary operational uses can embed the firm's distinctive data in continuous workflows. She advocates firm R&D departments because she expects technological evolution to continue. She also predicts increased use of secure shared workspaces where clients and outside counsel can access documents and AI simultaneously, reducing sequential review and redlining cycles. She does not offer a concrete prediction about partner retention in response to the host's question.

pts.k: Shaver predicts premium pricing for trusted judgment, some incumbent failures, growth of AI-native service firms and changes to the organizational scope of law firms.
pts.d: Her forecast shifts scarcity from lawyer time toward trusted judgment. She expects some firms to fail, more product companies to become AI-native service providers, and some legal partnerships to become businesses running multidisciplinary teams that combine legal and broader strategic services. She additionally predicts that a traditional firm will open an AI-native law-firm subsidiary. These are expressly forward-looking views, not documented outcomes. Her broader framing is that legal technology now affects business strategy and firms' growth or failure, rather than serving only a support function.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is principally Shaver's market observation, personal experience and secondhand examples, with some quantitative assertions but little methodological detail.
pts.d: For pricing and expanded capability, she cites an unnamed corporate project previously estimated at roughly $14 million and reports of firms mapping workflow reductions. For in-house adoption, she supplies doubling figures without identifying a dataset or method, plus an informal poll of approximately 100 GCs earlier in the year, without an exact response proportion. For workload and governance, she relies on personal experience and reports from firms, legal departments and acquaintances; the transcript supplies no systematic workload study or verified incident documentation. She invokes an agentic-systems book by Dan Katz and the Bommaritos for governance guidance. For daily use, she says data support her position without specifying results or design in her answer. The 37-hours-per-month figure and RSG/Harvey report framing are introduced by a host, not independently stated as Shaver's finding. Her cost, organizational and market forecasts are presented as judgments; the incumbent-disruption argument invokes Clayton Christensen's framework rather than a quantified failure forecast.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion is situated in 2026, with current observations, near-term cost and failure predictions, and longer-term organizational forecasts without fixed deadlines.
pts.d: Adoption comparisons cover 2024–2025 and end-2025 to the interview in 2026; the GC poll is described as earlier that year. Workflow changes were heard about over approximately the preceding year, and missing agent identifiers include reports from the previous year. Pricing change is selective by workflow and client preference, not universal. Governance requirements depend on the use case, third-party versus proprietary deployment, downstream access and risk level. Cost escalation is explicitly short term; backend optimization and AI's integration into work are eventual expectations. Firm failure is predicted for 'the next little while'; an AI-native subsidiary is predicted 'at some point.' Competitive differentiation is conditional on strategic operational investment beyond adoption, and Shaver does not assume every daily user will become a workflow builder.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law firms, corporate legal buyers, individual lawyers and staff, governance teams, and emerging AI-native providers.
pts.d: Traditional firms face margin pressure, opportunities for premium and newly feasible services, strategic differentiation requirements and possible failure. Large firms are described as having had more deployment resources than corporate legal departments initially. In-house teams can retain work, manage budgets and reconsider what they outsource; corporate clients may receive faster, broader and more valuable service. Lawyers and staff gain capacity but face higher work intensity and verification burdens. Technology, security and governance teams must manage agent traceability, permissions, supervision, policy enforcement and cost infrastructure. Product companies that begin delivering legal services are described as prospective AI-native competitors, distinct from vendors that merely sell software. Firm leaders and legal-technology professionals take on more strategic responsibilities, while some firms may move toward multidisciplinary service delivery. The document does not make a distinct access-to-justice or entry-level employment displacement claim.
